newsitem.title: UK: Reformist Russia starts to glitter for investors.
newsitem.headline: Reformist Russia starts to glitter for investors.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's determination to force Russia on to the road of reform and the choice of one of his toughest, if least popular, aides to do the job, are certain to prick the interest of foreign investors, analysts said on Monday.
Doubts linger about the implementation of promised reforms but the analysts said the past week's events gave them more confidence in Russia's future.

Late last week Yeltsin largely ended months of speculation over his health when he made a strong state of the nation speech, promising to fight crime and corruption, deal with massive fiscal problems and dilute the strength of monopolies.

To the delight of many outside the country, he also appointed as first deputy prime minister the tough reformist Anatoly Chubais, who was the architect of the world's largest privatisation programme during Yeltsin's first term in office.
"It's another push in the direction of reform," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's head of emerging market research, Paul Luke.
But analysts acknowledged that Chubais, who is much less popular at home, was a "kill or cure" appointment which could sit uneasily with other branches of the Russian establishment.

"If anybody is going to deal with (speeding up reform) it is going to be Chubais. But at the same time there is a problem of his unpopularity. I imagine there will be more trouble with parliament," said Vlad Sobell, senior economist at Daiwa Institute of Research.
"But the trend started this year in foreign investment will be boosted by his appointment," he added.

Sobell said that despite years of dashed hopes, there were some grounds this year for expecting a slight real rise in GDP, or at least stabilisation, after a long economic contraction since Russian reforms were launched.

"Russia has considerable potential for sustained rapid growth. Granted the right macroeconomic policies, regulatory framework and reasonably stable political scene, its economic growth could accelerate to about five percent a year by 2000," he said.

Chubais will be key in helping to deal with the overwhelming budgetary problems facing Russia, and the need to make spending cuts when so little can be done to increase revenue, West Merchant Bank strategist Ousmene Mandeng said.
"Public finance imbalances continue to represent the greatest source of economic instability," he said.

"Expenditure cuts targeting the pension system and housing sector...may be the only viable ways of addressing the fiscal problem in the shorter term. A more aggressive reform stance by Chubais may exactly do that," he added.

So far the market reaction has been subdued with prices of Russian debt firming in the past two trading days more because of the general rise in emerging debt markets that has followed the strength of U.S. Treasuries.

"Despite presistent economic difficulties, Russian debt at present prices is grossly undervalued. But most importantly for the expected price performance, Yeltsin's parliamentary address indicated that he is back in charge," Mandeng said.
